item: Every value has exactly one owner at a time, and that owner (a binding, a field, a container slot, a closure environment) is the single party responsible for running its destructor when it goes out of scope.
quote: There can only be one owner at a time.

item: A move copies only the inline bytes (for String: pointer, length, capacity) and statically invalidates the source, so the heap buffer is never duplicated and never freed twice; Rust never inserts an implicit deep copy, so any implicit copy is cheap by construction.
quote: But because Rust also invalidates the first variable, instead of being called a shallow copy, it’s known as a move.

item: Invalidation is a compile-time property of the place, not a runtime state of the value: a moved-from local is deinitialized, every read is rejected until it is assigned again, and reassigning a `let mut` binding after a move is legal and revives it.
quote: After moving out of a place expression that evaluates to a local variable, the location is deinitialized and cannot be read from again until it is reinitialized.

item: Loops are where moves bite: `for x in v` desugars to `IntoIterator::into_iter(v)` and consumes `v` (iterate `&v` or `&mut v` to borrow), and moving a non-Copy outer variable inside a loop body is rejected because the next iteration would read a deinitialized place, unless the body reassigns it or breaks.
quote: let result = match IntoIterator::into_iter(iter_expr) {

item: `Copy` means the implicit duplicate is a plain bitwise copy that cannot run user code and leaves the source usable; `Clone` is an explicit, possibly expensive call to arbitrary code, so the presence or absence of `.clone()` shows the reader where the cost is.
quote: Copy is not overloadable; it is always a simple bit-wise copy.

item: The compiler’s E0382 help text ("consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable") is a suggestion, not a fix; an expert first asks whether the callee should borrow (`&T`), whether the caller still needs the value, or whether ownership should be handed back by return.
quote: help: consider cloning the value if the performance cost is acceptable

item: A `.clone()` call does not always mean a deep copy: `Rc::clone` and `Arc::clone` only bump a reference count, which is why the convention `Rc::clone(&a)` is used to make shared-ownership handles visibly different from data copies.
quote: The call to Rc::clone only increments the reference count, which doesn’t take much time.
placement: a named later syllabus topic: 'Ownership topology over shared mutability'

item: `Copy` and `Drop` are mutually exclusive (E0184): a type that owns a resource beyond its own bytes cannot be duplicated bitwise, so any type with a destructor, or any field with one, always has move semantics.
quote: any type implementing Drop can’t be Copy, because it’s managing some resource besides its own size_of::<T> bytes.

item: Deriving `Copy` is a semver commitment: removing it later breaks every caller that relied on implicit copies, so a type that might later gain a heap field or a destructor should stay move-only from the start.
quote: implementing Copy is part of the public API of your type.

item: Shared references `&T` are `Copy` whatever `T` is, but `&mut T` is never `Copy`, because copying it would create two aliasing mutable references; this is why passing a `&mut` moves it (the reborrowing that hides this is covered with borrowing).
quote: copying &mut T would create an aliased mutable reference.
placement: here (implicit reborrowing of &mut belongs to Chapter 2, borrowing and lifetimes)

item: Signatures are ownership contracts that callers can read without opening the body: a `T` or `self` parameter consumes the argument, `&T`/`&self` borrows it, `&mut T`/`&mut self` borrows it exclusively, and returning `T` hands ownership back; a by-value `self` is the tool for "after this call the old value must not be used" (builders, `into_*`, state transitions).
quote: this technique is usually used when the method transforms self into something else and you want to prevent the caller from using the original instance after the transformation.

item: `&mut T` in a signature promises exclusivity, not just mutability: while it is live no other reference to the value may exist, which is what lets the callee mutate without the defensive copying or locking a C++ or Java programmer would add.
quote: If you have a mutable reference to a value, you can have no other references to that value.
placement: here (the full aliasing-XOR-mutation model and lifetimes are in Chapter 2, borrowing and lifetimes)

item: E0382 (use of moved value) has three labelled spans to read in order: where the value was moved, why it moved (its type is not `Copy`), and the later use; the fix depends on which of those three you change (borrow at the move site, derive Copy/Clone, or reorder or reassign before the use).
quote: A variable was used after its contents have been moved elsewhere.

item: E0505 (move out while borrowed) means a live borrow outlives the point where ownership leaves; because borrows end at their last use, the usual fix is to move the last use of the reference before the move, not to clone.
quote: Release borrow before move.

item: You cannot write `let s = v[i];` for a `Vec<String>`, because indexing a non-array type desugars to a dereference of the `&T` returned by `Index::index`, so `v[i]` is borrowed content (E0507); you take ownership with `remove`, `swap_remove`, `pop`, `into_iter`, or by putting something back.
quote: For other types an index expression a[b] is equivalent to *std::ops::Index::index(&a, b)

item: Through a `&mut` you may move a value out only if you leave a valid one in its place: `mem::replace`, `mem::take` and `Option::take` are the standard way out of E0507, and they are central to working with `&mut self` in real code.
quote: It is fine only if you put something back. mem::replace can be used for that:

item: Only some places can be moved out of: unborrowed locals, temporaries, `*box`, and fields of such places whose containing type does not implement `Drop`; moving a field out of a `Drop` type is E0509 because its destructor needs the whole value.
quote: Fields of a place expression which can be moved out of and don’t implement Drop.
placement: a named later syllabus topic: 'Partial moves and destructuring as transfer'

item: Moving a `Box<T>` moves one pointer no matter how large `T` is, so boxing is the standard way to make a large value cheap to move, and `*b` is a place you are allowed to move out of, unlike other smart pointers.
quote: only the small amount of pointer data is copied around on the stack

item: A move of a large by-value type is a real memory copy (above roughly 128 bytes, a `memcpy` call), and the optimizer is not guaranteed to remove it, so large structs, arrays and big enum variants passed or returned by value have a measurable cost that `size_of` and profiling expose.
quote: Rust types that are larger than 128 bytes are copied with memcpy rather than inline code.

item: Rust has no move constructor: a move is always a byte copy with no user hook, and a value’s address can change at any move, so code must never rely on a value staying at a stable address unless it is pinned.
quote: The compiler is allowed to move a value to a new address without running any code to notify that value that its address has changed.

item: Unlike C++ `std::move`, which is only a cast that hands the object to a user-written move constructor and leaves a moved-from object that is still destroyed and must stay valid, a Rust move ends the source binding statically, runs no destructor on it, and needs no "null out the source" code.
quote: Assign the data members of the source object to default values. This prevents the destructor from freeing resources (such as memory) multiple times:

item: Conditional moves (moving in one branch only) are legal: when the compiler cannot know statically whether a value is still owned at scope end, it keeps a hidden drop flag on the stack and checks it at run time to decide whether to drop.
quote: As a variable becomes initialized and uninitialized, a drop flag for that variable is toggled.
placement: a named later syllabus topic: 'RAII, drop order, and leak safety' (state here only that conditional moves compile and stay sound)

item: Closures are owners too: `move` makes a closure capture by value (needed for `thread::spawn` and returned closures), but which `Fn` trait it implements depends on what the body does with the captures; only a body that moves a capture out is limited to `FnOnce`, and moving out of a capture in an `Fn`/`FnMut` closure is E0507.
quote: the traits implemented by a closure type are determined by what the closure does with captured values, not how it captures them

item: Patterns move: `match opt { Some(s) => .. }` or `let (a, b) = pair;` moves non-Copy parts out of the scrutinee and leaves it unusable, while `_` binds nothing and moves nothing, and matching on `&opt` switches the default binding mode to `ref` so nothing moves.
quote: Unlike identifier patterns, it does not copy, move, or borrow the value it matches.
placement: a named later syllabus topic: 'Partial moves and destructuring as transfer' (mention here that a match can move out of its scrutinee)
